# Nemotron 3 Ultra makes the case for fast, open coding models
- [CodeRabbit Benchmark Performance](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/nemotron-3-ultra-release#heading-coderabbit-benchmark-performance)

## What we know about Nemotron 3 Ultra
The cleanest comparison is with [Nemotron 3 Super](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/faster-code-reviews-with-nemotron-3-super), the previous large model in the family.

| Characteristic | Nemotron 3 Super | Nemotron 3 Ultra |
|-|-|-|
| Total parameters | 120B | 550B |
| Architecture | Hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE | Hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE |
| Expert design | Latent MoE | Latent MoE |
| Context length | Up to 1M tokens | Up to 1M tokens |

Artificial Analysis also reported more than 300 output tokens per second on a pre-release DeepInfra endpoint.

## CodeRabbit Benchmark Performance
CodeRabbit's internal benchmark gives a more grounded view than launch charts alone. The benchmark compares a baseline set of review models against a Nemotron 3 Ultra configuration across 105 evaluation problems, ranging from easier issues to harder review tasks. The evaluation uses post-pipeline final comments after verification, deduplication, and assertive filtering. The judge was gpt-5.1 with medium reasoning, low verbosity, single mode, and three votes.

![CodeRabbit benchmark table compares Baseline average and Nematron 3 Ultra performance metrics.](https://www.coderabbit.ai/content/assets/image4-6.png)

The top-line result is close:

- Baseline average, N=3: 60/105 pass actual, or 57 percent
- Nemotron 3 Ultra average, N=2: 58/105 pass actual, or 56 percent
- Baseline pass full: 66/105, or 63 percent
- Nemotron 3 Ultra pass full: 65/105, or 62 percent
- Baseline precision actual: 34.0 percent
- Nemotron 3 Ultra precision actual: 33.0 percent

## Where Ultra looks strong for developers
The strongest use case for Nemotron 3 Ultra is not "replace every coding model."

## What developers should watch out for
Give it a checklist.

## Verdict
It is chasing usable throughput.

The model is big, open, and fast. Public benchmarks put it near the top of US open-weight intelligence while keeping it far ahead of many peers on output speed. CodeRabbit's benchmark adds a more sober picture: Ultra can perform close to a strong review baseline, but it currently needs retries and external validation for structured-output reliability.

For coding teams, the bigger story is not whether Nemotron 3 Ultra replaces a favorite chat model. It is whether open, high-throughput coding agents are starting to feel practical.

- [Verdict](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/nemotron-3-ultra-release#heading-verdict)

[Back to blog](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog)

![Cover image](https://www.coderabbit.ai/_next/image?url=%2Fcontent%2Fassets%2Fnemotron-3-ultra-juan.png&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_2dK6z4U2VCFVDyeWDXp4QiDfUjU2)

NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra does not feel like another model built primarily for a chat window. The first question is not whether it can win a leaderboard, but whether it can fit into the way developers actually use models now: inside terminals, review pipelines, coding agents, test generators, and workflows where the model has to keep moving through messy context.

[NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/) is releasing a large open model with roughly 550 billion total parameters and about 55 billion active per token, but the real pitch is speed plus control. If a model is fast enough, a developer can stay in the loop. A system can retry it. A coding harness can keep it working until the task is actually finished.

Ultra is not the model I would frame as "the new best coding assistant." It points toward a world where open models become fast, controllable workers inside developer systems, not just chat interfaces waiting for the next prompt.

For workflows where the model is one part of a larger loop, Nemotron 3 Ultra becomes especially relevant: code review, test generation, repository research, agentic coding, and internal automation where teams care about speed, control, and where the model runs.

![Scatter plot showing AI intelligence index versus output speed, with a most attractive quadrant highlighted.](https://www.coderabbit.ai/content/assets/image-1.png)

## What we know about Nemotron 3 Ultra

Nemotron 3 Ultra is the largest model in [NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 family](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/coderabbit-ai-code-reviews-now-support-nvidia-nemotron). The family includes Nano, Super, and Ultra, all designed around agentic AI applications. Ultra is the big reasoning engine in that lineup: roughly 550 billion total parameters, with about 55 billion active per token through a sparse mixture-of-experts design.

The cleanest comparison is with [Nemotron 3 Super](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/faster-code-reviews-with-nemotron-3-super), the previous large model in the family.

| Characteristic | Nemotron 3 Super | Nemotron 3 Ultra |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Role in the family | High-throughput reasoning model for agentic workflows | Largest Nemotron 3 reasoning model for more complex coding, research, and enterprise workflows |
| Total parameters | 120B | 550B |
| Active parameters | 12B active per token | 55B active per token |
| Architecture | Hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE | Hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE |
| Expert design | Latent MoE | Latent MoE |
| Context length | Up to 1M tokens | Up to 1M tokens |
| Efficiency features | Multi-token prediction and NVFP4 training/deployment path | Multi-token prediction and NVFP4-oriented deployment path |
| Best fit | High-volume agentic workflows, coding, planning, and tool use | More demanding developer workflows where speed, scale, and stronger reasoning need to sit in the same loop |

In simpler terms: this is not just a bigger dense Transformer. Ultra is built to activate only part of the network per token, keep long context practical, and produce tokens quickly enough that developers can use it interactively instead of treating it like a slow background batch job.

![Flowchart detailing Nemotron 3 Ultra's fast architecture: long context, Mamba-Transformer, MoE routing, multi-token prediction.](https://www.coderabbit.ai/content/assets/image1-19.png)

The launch numbers put Ultra in a strong spot. [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/) reported Nemotron 3 Ultra at 48 on its Intelligence Index, making it the leading US open-weight model in that snapshot, ahead of Gemma 4 31B, Nemotron 3 Super, and gpt-oss-120b. Kimi K2.6 still sits higher at 54, so the claim is not that Ultra owns the entire open frontier. The claim is that it is unusually fast for the intelligence level it reaches.

Artificial Analysis also reported more than 300 output tokens per second on a pre-release DeepInfra endpoint. For developers, that speed is the useful part. In coding, latency changes behavior. If a model is slow, you fire and forget. If it is fast, you stay in the loop, ask follow-ups, run multiple attempts, and let an agentic harness keep pushing.

![NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra announcement slide showing a cost comparison graph presented by a speaker.](https://www.coderabbit.ai/content/assets/image3-9.png)

## What is different this time

Nemotron 3 Super already showed that NVIDIA could build a capable open model for agentic workflows. Ultra pushes further in two ways.

First, it is much bigger. Super is around 120B total parameters with roughly 12B active. Ultra moves to roughly 550B total and 55B active. That extra scale shows up in the way NVIDIA and early testers talk about it: not as a small efficient helper model, but as a model that can start taking work from proprietary frontier systems in selected workflows.

Second, Ultra appears to have been trained and evaluated with developer harnesses more directly in mind. NVIDIA mentions that Super turned out to be good in agentic harnesses, while Ultra was built with those harnesses in mind. For coding tools, that changes the requirements. A model that works well in OpenCode, OpenHands, Kilo Code, Continue, or an internal code review loop has to do more than answer questions. It has to follow tool protocols, manage long context, make progress under repeated prompts, and recover when it gets stuck.

Ultra's behavior fits that target. The model is quick, direct, not especially verbose, and unlikely to ask for lots of clarification. That can be a strength in a harness, but a weakness if the task depends on unstated requirements. It benefits from explicit instruction. The best mental model is closer to Codex-style prompting than Claude-style prompting. Spell out the task. Give acceptance criteria. State the expected output format.

## CodeRabbit Benchmark Performance

CodeRabbit's internal benchmark gives a more grounded view than launch charts alone. The benchmark compares a baseline set of review models against a Nemotron 3 Ultra configuration across 105 evaluation problems, ranging from easier issues to harder review tasks. The evaluation uses post-pipeline final comments after verification, deduplication, and assertive filtering. The judge was gpt-5.1 with medium reasoning, low verbosity, single mode, and three votes.

![CodeRabbit benchmark table compares Baseline average and Nematron 3 Ultra performance metrics.](https://www.coderabbit.ai/content/assets/image4-6.png)

The top-line result is close:

- Baseline average, N=3: 60/105 pass actual, or 57 percent
- Nemotron 3 Ultra average, N=2: 58/105 pass actual, or 56 percent
- Baseline pass full: 66/105, or 63 percent
- Nemotron 3 Ultra pass full: 65/105, or 62 percent
- Baseline precision actual: 34.0 percent
- Nemotron 3 Ultra precision actual: 33.0 percent

The positive read: on this review workload, Ultra was roughly in the same band as the baseline on pass metrics. It found real issues, survived the review pipeline, and produced useful CodeRabbit-style comments.

The caveat is reliability. The model had a high retry rate. The benchmark summary shows an average of 36.5 retries for the Ultra runs, compared with 0.3 for the baseline. The retry distribution notes that about 66 percent were scratchpad-only. In practice, the model sometimes voluntarily stops before producing the required output marker or final structured output. Retrying without changing the prompt often works, which suggests the capability is there, but the first-attempt completion behavior is not stable enough to ignore.

The practical finding from the CodeRabbit data is clear: Nemotron 3 Ultra can do the work, but it should be wrapped in validation and retry logic for structured-output tasks.

There is also an interesting latency signal. In the benchmark, the Ultra run shows a mean latency of 7:06 per full review trace, compared with 8:31 for the baseline. That is not an enormous difference in this specific report, but the Ultra runs were carrying a large retry burden and still remained competitive on time. NVIDIA's framing around Ultra repeatedly returns to the same idea: if the model is fast enough, several attempts can still beat one slower, more careful attempt.

The cost story is less clean in the benchmark. The reported total cost for the Ultra run is higher than the baseline in this specific table. That should not be over-generalized, because internal fallback rates, hosted endpoint pricing, and retry behavior can dominate a local experiment. The public NVIDIA and Artificial Analysis story is about cost-to-completion and throughput. The [CodeRabbit](https://www.coderabbit.ai/) results say something narrower: on this benchmark, quality was close, speed was competitive, and the reliability control loop needs work.

## Where Ultra looks strong for developers

The strongest use case for Nemotron 3 Ultra is not "replace every coding model." It is "run a lot of useful developer work quickly, with explicit instructions and external checks."

It looks promising for:

- Code review pipelines where comments can be verified, filtered, deduplicated, and retried
- Integration test generation, especially when the model needs to read broad context
- Repository research tasks that require scanning many files or documents
- Agentic workflows where a harness can keep the model moving until the task is complete
- Everyday coding tasks that benefit from fast iteration more than perfect one-shot reasoning

NVIDIA also shared a useful example: Ultra was used in OpenCode to read several papers and reason across them. That is not a PhD-level coding challenge, but it is exactly the kind of everyday developer task where speed changes the workflow. You can stay in the terminal, watch the model move, and keep steering.

For CodeRabbit-style work, the model also seems especially interesting on easier and medium-difficulty review tasks. These are still valuable reviews: the system needs to catch practical issues, explain them clearly, and produce a lot of review output without waiting on a more expensive frontier model every time.

## What developers should watch out for

Ultra needs structure. If you are using it for coding or developer automation, do not treat it as a free-form chat model and hope it infers the workflow. Give it a harness. Give it a checklist. Give it stop conditions. Give it output validation.

Practical guidance:

- Use explicit prompts with concrete acceptance criteria.
- For structured output, validate the required markers or schema before accepting the response.
- Add retry logic for premature stops.
- Use goal loops or external completion checks so the model keeps working until the task is actually done.
- Ask for tests explicitly. In early hands-on use, the model did not always generate its own tests.
- Be specific about design requirements. It can produce better visual artifacts than expected, but design is not its core strength.
- Prefer it for high-throughput workflows where several attempts are acceptable.
- Be cautious for workflows where a single malformed output can break production automation.

This model also changes how teams should think about benchmarking. A pure one-shot benchmark may underrate Ultra if the real product loop allows retries. A benchmark that ignores retries may overrate it if the product needs strict first-attempt formatting. The right metric is probably closer to time-to-usable-completion, with quality, retries, latency, and cost all measured together.

## Verdict

Nemotron 3 Ultra is one of the most interesting open model releases for developers because it is not only chasing intelligence. It is chasing usable throughput.

The model is big, open, and fast. Public benchmarks put it near the top of US open-weight intelligence while keeping it far ahead of many peers on output speed. CodeRabbit's benchmark adds a more sober picture: Ultra can perform close to a strong review baseline, but it currently needs retries and external validation for structured-output reliability.

The verdict is nuanced. If you want a model that will nail every strict format on the first try, Ultra is not yet the safest default. If you are building an agentic developer system where the harness can validate, retry, and keep pressure on the model until the work is complete, Ultra becomes much more compelling.

For coding teams, the bigger story is not whether Nemotron 3 Ultra replaces a favorite chat model. It is whether open, high-throughput coding agents are starting to feel practical.

#### [Models](https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nvidia-nemotron-v3) [Ultra Tech Report](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/files/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-Technical-Report.pdf) [Nemotron 3 Blog](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/Nemotron-3/)
We present our most capable model yet – Nemotron 3 Ultra with 550 billion total and 55 billion active parameters. Nemotron 3 Ultra is the final and best model of the [**Nemotron 3 family of models**](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/Nemotron-3/).

### Key Highlights
![Comparison](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/images/nvidia-nemotron-3-ultra/ultra-3-comparison.png)

- Nemotron 3 Ultra achieves **5.9x, 4.8x, and 1.6x higher inference throughput compared to GLM-5.1-754B-A40B, Kimi-K2.6-1T-A32B, and Qwen-3.5-397B-17B respectively** on the 8k token input / 64k token output setting.
- Nemotron 3 Ultra achieves **on-par accuracies compared to other state-of-the-art open LLMs** across a diverse set of benchmarks.

### Open Source
#### Checkpoints:
- [**Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B-A55B NVFP4**](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-NVFP4): post-trained and NVFP4 quantized model
- [**Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B-A55B BF16**](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-BF16): post-trained model
- [**Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B-A55B Base BF16**](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-Base-BF16): base model
- [**Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B-A55B GenRM**](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-GenRM): GenRM used for RLHF

#### [Models](https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nvidia-nemotron-v3) [Ultra Tech Report](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/files/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-Technical-Report.pdf) [Nemotron 3 Blog](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/Nemotron-3/)

![Nemotron 3 Ultra Overview](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/images/nvidia-nemotron-3-ultra/ultra-3-aa.png)

We present our most capable model yet – Nemotron 3 Ultra with 550 billion total and 55 billion active parameters. Nemotron 3 Ultra is the final and best model of the [**Nemotron 3 family of models**](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/Nemotron-3/).

### Key Features

1. Employs **Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Attention architecture**.
2. Leverages [**LatentMoE**](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/LatentMoE/) for improved accuracy.
3. Includes **MTP layers** for faster inference through native speculative decoding.
4. Supports inference time **reasoning budget control**.
5. Pretrained in **NVFP4**.
6. Post-trained with enhanced pipeline involving **Supervised Fine Tuning (SFT)**, **Reinforcement Learning (RL)**, and **Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD)** for improved model accuracy.

### Key Highlights

![Comparison](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/images/nvidia-nemotron-3-ultra/ultra-3-comparison.png)

- Nemotron 3 Ultra achieves **5.9x, 4.8x, and 1.6x higher inference throughput compared to GLM-5.1-754B-A40B, Kimi-K2.6-1T-A32B, and Qwen-3.5-397B-17B respectively** on the 8k token input / 64k token output setting.
- Nemotron 3 Ultra achieves **on-par accuracies compared to other state-of-the-art open LLMs** across a diverse set of benchmarks.
- Supports **context length of up to 1M tokens** while outperforming state-of-the-art open LLMs on RULER at 1M context length.

### Open Source

We are releasing the pre-trained, post-trained, and quantized checkpoints along with the datasets used for training.

#### Checkpoints:

- [**Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B-A55B NVFP4**](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-NVFP4): post-trained and NVFP4 quantized model
- [**Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B-A55B BF16**](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-BF16): post-trained model
- [**Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B-A55B Base BF16**](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-Base-BF16): base model
- [**Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B-A55B GenRM**](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-GenRM): GenRM used for RLHF

#### Data:

- [**Nemotron-Pretraining-Code-v3**](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-Pretraining-Code-v3): 173B tokens of fresh code data from GitHub through September 30, 2025.
- [**Nemotron-Pretraining-Legal-v1**](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-Pretraining-Legal-v1): A collection of synthetic datasets intended to improve the legal capabilities of LLMs.
- [**Nemotron-Pretraining-Specialized-v1.2**](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-Pretraining-Specialized-v1.2): A collection of synthetic datasets aimed to improve LLM capabilities on factual recall, moral scenarios, and diverse generative and multiple choice questions.
- [**Nemotron-Posttraining-v3**](https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nemotron-post-training-v3): A collection of post-training datasets for improving agentic, reasoning, and general model capabilities during SFT and RL.

#### Model Recipes:

- [**NVIDIA Nemotron Developer Repository**](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Nemotron)

#### Tech Report

More technical details in the [Tech Report](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/files/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-Technical-Report.pdf)

## Transcript

Over the past year, the narrative in
open weights LLMs has been that Chinese
labs are winning. The Kimmy models, ZAI
models, MiniMax have all had these big
impressive models. But in an attempt to
take back that crown, Nvidia has just
dropped a 550 billion parameter model
that beats many of these trillion
parameter models on agent benchmarks.
And more importantly, they published
exactly how they did it. If you're
building agents, this may just be a
game-changer for which open models you
should be reaching for. So naturally,
when Nvidia reached out to me to sponsor
a video, this is the one that I wanted
to get access to. And in this video, I'm
going to show you the actual numbers,
not just the marketing. We're going to
break down some of the recipes of how
they've actually made this model. And
then we'll have a play with the model to
see exactly how this holds up. So
Nvidia's been working hard on making a
whole suite of open models. So I've
covered a few of the Nemotron models on
the channel. For the Nemotron 3 series,
they started with the nano model, which
was at the end of last year. And the
nano model was all about being a small,
fast, high-efficiency kind of model.
Earlier this year, they released
Nemotron 3 super. And that was really
built for multi-agent applications. So
that one really took off with things
like open claw and stuff like that. And
that brings us to today, where they're
rolling out Nemotron 3 ultra. Now,
Nemotron 3 ultra is their most capable
model yet. It's the flagship model that
they've been working on for a while.
This is not a small model. It's probably
not a model that you can even run
locally. But it certainly is a model
that companies will be able to use on
prem, be able to fine-tune for their use
tasks, that kind of thing. So Nemotron 3
ultra is certainly a beast of a model.
We're talking about a model that's 550
billion parameters mixture of experts
model with 55 billion parameters active.
And the goal with this is that it's been
trained again for agentic uses. So, this
model is made not to be any sort of
chatbot. This is an agentic model where
it can write, it can use tools, it can
code, and it can do long horizon many
step actions. Just like we've seen with
some of the Chinese open models like the
Qwen 2.6, etc. You can really think of
Nemotron Ultra as Nvidia's attempt at
making these huge models. That while it
is really big, it's trying to get on par
with some of the frontier labs and some
of the performance of models like
Anthropic Opus, the recent GPT series,
the sort of Gemini Pro kind of models.
Now, for me again, what sets this apart,
just like I talked about recently in the
Nemotron Omni video, is that it's not
just the model that's really interesting
thing here. It's the fact that they're
actually openly talking about how it was
made. The fact that they've released
data sets, the fact that it looks like
we've got recipes for what they actually
did here, means that if you do want to
take this model and fine-tune it for a
very specific task for an organization.
And I should stress that nowadays more
and more what I'm seeing is big
organizations taking some of these open
models, often the Chinese open weights
models, but also things like Gemma 4 and
the Nemotron models, and then basically
fine-tuning them to have custom
that are really good for the company's
specific use tasks to replace
proprietary models, whether that's from
Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, etc. If you
listen to the VentureBeat podcast that I
do, recently we've had people on from
LinkedIn and from Pinterest, from a
number of these different really big
companies talking about doing exactly
that, where they're taking these open
weights models, customizing them for
their very specific use cases and then
serving them at scale for millions if
not hundreds of millions of users. I
think for LinkedIn it's over a billion
users for what they've been doing with
some of the small open weights models.
So one of the techniques that NVIDIA has
used to create NeMo Triton 3 Ultra is
exactly one of the techniques that
LinkedIn told us about on the podcast.
And this is this whole idea of
multi-teacher on-policy distillation.
And the idea here that you take a very
strong base model. So they train up like
the NeMo Triton base model. They then
train one version of it for code. They
train one version for tool use, one
version for instruction following and
stuff like that. And then what they do
is they distill from each of these
teachers that they've trained up to be
really good at specific things onto one
final model. So the advantage there is
that you're getting basically these
strong teachers that are very strong at
what they've been sort of taught to be
strong at. But then you're able to use
those to distill them down to the final
model that is able to be good at all of
these things. Now what actually happens
there is it turns out that by training
the separate teachers and then
distilling down, you actually get a
model that's much stronger than just
taking the one model and training it on
all of those things. And one of the cool
things here is that this can be done in
sort of an RL fashion where once you've
basically got that teacher, it can
actually sort of coax this out of the
base model as it goes along. Now another
thing that NVIDIA has focused on with
NeMo Triton 3 Ultra is this whole idea
of post-training for agent harnesses. So
the idea here is that as agent
harnesses, whether that's Open Claw,
whether that's Hermes, whether that's
some kind of LangChain deep agents,
etc., They create these trajectories.
And if you train the model on those
trajectories and train them specifically
for task completion of these, so you
give them things like where perhaps
they're going to get things wrong, they
learn to be able to backtrack, they
learn to be able to fix errors by using
the harness, by using the different tool
calls, by using perhaps some kind of
memory, etc. This just allows the model
to be much, much stronger at these
particular kind of agentic tasks. Now,
another thing is that this is often done
in some kind of RL environments. That's
one of the cool things that Nvidia's
been talking about is actually opening
up a lot of these data sets and the
actual RL environments. So, we know, for
example, that RL environments were the
things that sort of made the Chinchilla
2.5, the Minimax 2.7 models, you know,
the GLM models around that time all have
this sort of lift-off where they
suddenly got a lot better. That was
coming because of the RL environments.
With Nvidia opening up a lot of these RL
environments, and I've got to stress
that as I'm recording this, I haven't
had a chance to play with all of those.
That's something that maybe I will look
at in the future. But with them opening
this up, people are actually going to be
able to see how these things are being
made and how these things are actually
being used for different kinds of
post-training on a large model like
this. And usually that kind of thing is
something that, you know, the different
model companies don't want to make
public. From what I've read so far,
Nvidia plans on releasing a lot of these
different environments, which is
definitely a huge win for the
open-source community. Even if you don't
end up using this model, there is a good
chance that you will end up using a
smaller version of some model that was
trained on some of these data sets and
with some of these RL environments. I
should also point out that the model
itself actually is like a hybrid mixture
of experts architecture. It's actually
supporting things like multi-token
prediction. It's got a million context
window. And while you're probably going
to need something like, you know,
multiple H100s or a B200 to be able to
actually run this, you are certainly
going to see this being served by a lot
of the inference companies that are out
there. And my guess is they'll see them
making it available for fine-tuning,
etc. Okay, so when we come and look at
the benchmarks for this, you can see
that Nemotron 3 Ultra is doing very well
for a lot of the different tasks. Now,
that doesn't mean that it's actually
winning for all the tasks in here, but
look at this. This is a 550 billion
parameter model. It's comparing to
models that are actually much bigger
than it. The Qwen 3.5 model it easily
beats. It would have been nice to see it
being compared to some of the newer Qwen
models, which have also had a lot more
RLL environment training. And I think
that's one of the key things that's
going on here. If you look at the GLM
5.1, which I covered before, this model
was heavily post-trained on these RLL
environments. And even then, Nemotron
Ultra is doing better than the 1
trillion parameter model. It does make
me wonder if someone actually just takes
this and runs it on a lot more of these
RLL environments, would we see a
substantial bump in the actual results
here? Now, of course, the biggest
advantage of being smaller than the
other models means that you're going to
be faster than the other models. You can
see here, this is from Artificial
Analysis team, where they Nemotron 3
Ultra is getting over 300 tokens per
second, much faster than the Kimmy and
the GLM models. Finally, if we come in
and look at PinchBench, so this is a
benchmark that's basically geared
towards agent harnesses like Open Claw,
you can see that while Anthropic is best
overall, the best open weights model
here actually is this Nvidia Neumotron 3
Ultra. And you can see coming in and
looking at this that the Ultra model
really isn't that far behind the
proprietary models like the Claude Opus
4.8 in here. So, knowing that you're
getting a much cheaper model here, this
definitely makes sense that Nvidia is
positioning this as a model that people
can use for running their agents both
cheaply and efficiently. So, let's jump
into a notebook and have a look at how
this actually works for reasoning and
tool calling. Okay, so I'll quickly just
go through a quick demo of using this.
And as always, I'll put the notebook in
the description. You can have a play
with it yourself. So, I'm actually
running this from Nvidia's cloud. So,
basically you just need to set up an
account and put in your Nvidia API key
in there. But, you certainly don't need
to run it here. You'll find this model
on open router. You'll find it on a lot
of the different inference providers.
So, really pick the one that you're most
comfortable with, I would say there. All
right, we've just got then some
streaming and some helper functions in
here for just doing this. We also want
to set up some tools for basically
testing things out. So, we've got a
calculator tool. We've got kind of like
a little rag tool, but basically we can
ask it about GPU specs since this is
Nvidia and it will basically return back
a bunch of information there. And you'll
notice that everything that we're doing
for sort of tool definitions and stuff
like that is in the OpenAI sort of
format. And the model's being built so
that it can use an OpenAI API endpoint,
you know, very simply. All right, the
key things here is this is a reasoning
model, but you've got different options
with the reasoning. So, you can see here
that we can basically just pass in
enable thinking equals true. And you'll
see in this case we've got a helper
function printing out the thinking in
green. You can see that okay, we've got
all the thinking for this simple test,
and then it comes to the answer. And it
just basically prints out the answer
there. Now, you've also got the ability
to be able to set the level of thinking
that you want. So, this can be low
effort of where you basically just got
short reasoning. This is for when you
want a a low cost, a low latency, and
stuff like that. You then got default
thinking, which the model itself will
actually decide how long the chain of
thought is going to be. And then we've
got a reasoning budget, so you can
actually explicitly sort of tell it,
"Okay, this is the number of thinking
tokens that I want you to sort of max
out at." Now, even though you can see
here I've set that to 16,000, in my
testing very rarely it will even get
close to that kind of budget here. It
does seem to be very succinct in its
reasoning. So, you can see here if we
look at the output. We've got the low
effort one where we've got a certain
amount of reasoning, and then we've got
the answer coming out. The default one,
we've got a certain amount of reasoning,
and then the answer out. And then we've
got our longer one. Now, if you actually
look at these, we can see that okay, the
approximate amount of reasoning tokens,
yes, went up. But the interesting thing
here is that the default one, in this
case the default one's actually longer
than the sort of budget one that we set
here. So, I've given it another one here
that's not a mathematical kind of thing.
It's much more sort of, you know, a
thinking thing. And you can see that
sure enough on this one, we had the low
effort be only about 100 tokens, the
default one a little bit under 200, and
then the budgeted one where we've said,
you know, go for a long amount of time,
it's still only going to sort of 200
tokens. So, my testing, this kind of
fits for when you want a model just to
basically get to the point and give you
an answer back very quickly. All right,
we can do the same thing with sort of
tool calls. You can see here, we're
basically getting it some tools. These
were the tools that we defined earlier
on. So, we've got some tools about GPU
specs and how much power they're using.
We're asking it to basically calculate
this out. So, we've passed in a
calculator. We've passed in the GPU
spec. You can see here that it's done a
pretty good job at deciding, okay, this
is the tool that it's going to use. This
is the arguments for that tool. Then, we
get the response back. In round two,
it's going to basically use the
calculator tool. It's going to decide,
okay, what it's going to actually put
into that calculator tool. And then
finally, in round three, it's basically
just going through not using any tools.
It's just giving us the answer back. And
you can see it does a quite a nice job
at that. So, the model is certainly good
at doing these agentic runs of where you
want it to basically run a bunch of
tools, be able to use those outputs,
process them, and to be able to work out
what the next tool would be that makes
sense for this particular agent use
case. So, overall, this is definitely
what you want for things like your Open
Claw, Nano Claw, your Hermes agent, that
kind of thing, where you've got an agent
that you're injecting lots of tools in.
You want to be able to get, you know,
the various responses out, etc. So,
overall, I would say check out. This is
certainly a model that, while I
necessarily wouldn't use it as my
top-tier model for everything, if you
want to run a sort of personal agent,
single-tenant user agent, this is
definitely a good model for that. And it
makes a lot of sense to do this because
it's both very quick, it's reliable,
it's got the reasoning that you need,
but it's not going to break the bank
like some of the frontier models. And
like I said earlier on in the video, for
me, probably the biggest thing about
this is not just the model itself, it's
that NVIDIA is making these training
recipes available, they're making data
available, they're making it possible
for lots of companies to not only see
how this was done, but to be able to
take this and work on their own
versions, which I think is a huge win
for open weights models and for open
LLMs in general. So, as always, let me
know in the comments what you think. If
you've got any questions or anything,
found the video useful, please click
like and subscribe, and I will talk to
you in the next video. Bye for now.
